related_questions.question: What is the #1 cause of pancreatic cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: While there isn't a single, universally identified cause of pancreatic cancer, tobacco use (smoking) is the leading modifiable risk factor. People who smoke are twice as likely to develop pancreatic cancer compared to non-smokers. Other significant risk factors include obesity, chronic pancreatitis, and a family history of pancreatic cancer.

list.title: Smoking:
list.snippet: Cigarette smoking is linked to a substantial percentage of pancreatic cancer cases and is considered the most significant preventable risk factor.

list.title: Obesity:
list.snippet: Being overweight or obese increases the risk of developing pancreatic cancer.

list.title: Chronic Pancreatitis:
list.snippet: Persistent inflammation of the pancreas can significantly elevate the risk.

list.title: Family History:
list.snippet: A family history of pancreatic cancer, especially in close relatives, increases an individual's risk.

list.title: Other Factors:
list.snippet: Diabetes, older age (over 65), certain genetic syndromes, and potentially a diet high in red and processed meats can also play a role.

related_questions.question: What is the new treatment for pancreatic cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: Several promising new treatments for pancreatic cancer are currently in development or have recently been approved. These include new chemotherapy combinations like NALIRIFOX, personalized mRNA vaccines, and targeted therapies like BIZENGRI (zenocutuzumab-zbco) for specific gene alterations. Immunotherapy is also showing promise, with clinical trials exploring its potential to boost the immune system's response against pancreatic cancer.
snippet_highlighted_words: new chemotherapy combinations like NALIRIFOX, personalized mRNA vaccines, and targeted therapies like BIZENGRI (zenocutuzumab-zbco) for specific gene alterations

list.snippet: NALIRIFOX: This new chemotherapy regimen is a first-line treatment option for metastatic pancreatic cancer. It has shown improved overall survival compared to the older standard, gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel.

list.title: mRNA vaccines:
list.snippet: Clinical trials are investigating personalized mRNA vaccines, like autogene cevumeran, that can stimulate the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells, potentially reducing the risk of recurrence after surgery.

list.title: Checkpoint inhibitors and other immunotherapy approaches:
list.snippet: Research is ongoing to combine immunotherapy drugs, such as checkpoint inhibitors, with other therapies like chemotherapy and CXCR4 inhibitors to enhance the immune response against pancreatic cancer.

list.title: BIZENGRI (zenocutuzumab-zbco):
list.snippet: This drug is approved for patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma who have a specific NRG1 gene fusion and whose cancer has progressed after previous treatments.

list.title: CABOMETYX (cabozantinib):
list.snippet: Approved for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) and extra-pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, which are different from the more common pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).

list.title: Targeting cancer cell metabolism:
list.snippet: Researchers are exploring ways to target the unique metabolic processes of pancreatic cancer cells.

list.title: Surgery for initially inoperable patients:
list.snippet: There are ongoing efforts to expand the criteria for surgical intervention in patients initially deemed inoperable.

Many of these new treatments are being evaluated in clinical trials, and it's important for patients to discuss these options with their doctors to determine if they are eligible for participation in a trial.

list.title: Metastatic vs. early-stage disease:
list.snippet: Treatment approaches can vary depending on whether the cancer has spread (metastatic) or is still localized.

list.title: Specific genetic mutations:
list.snippet: Targeted therapies are often designed to address specific genetic mutations or alterations in cancer cells, so genetic testing is crucial.

list.title: Individual patient characteristics:
list.snippet: Treatment decisions should always be made in consultation with a medical professional, taking into account the individual patient's overall health, stage of the disease, and other factors.

related_questions.question: What is the life expectancy of someone with pancreatic cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: The life expectancy for someone with pancreatic cancer varies significantly based on the stage at diagnosis and individual factors. Generally, the five-year survival rate is low, around 10% for all stages combined, but localized cancers have a much higher survival rate (27.1%). The average patient with late-stage pancreatic cancer lives about one year after diagnosis.
snippet_highlighted_words: the five-year survival rate is low, around 10% for all stages combined, but localized cancers have a much higher survival rate (27.1%)

list.title: Localized Cancer:
list.snippet: If the cancer is found early and hasn't spread, the five-year survival rate can be as high as 44%.

list.title: Regional Cancer:
list.snippet: When the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes or tissues, the five-year survival rate drops to around 10.7%.

list.title: Distant Metastatic Cancer:
list.snippet: When the cancer has spread to distant organs, the five-year survival rate is only about 2.4%.
Stage at diagnosis: Early detection offers the best chance of successful treatment.
Overall health: Age, other medical conditions, and lifestyle choices can affect outcomes.
Treatment received: Surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy can play a significant role in extending life.
Tumor characteristics: Size, type, and spread of the tumor all affect prognosis.
